planting.note: Transplant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring into well-drained soil under high canopy or dappled light.

directions: This small, vase-shaped maple from Japan shows off blue-green and white striped bark that stands out all winter long, a trait it shares with the snakebark maple group. Give it filtered or open shade, since its thin bark can scorch in hot afternoon sun, and water occasionally once established. The small leaves turn clean gold and orange in fall and drop quickly, making cleanup simple. It stays naturally compact, so little pruning is needed beyond removing crossing branches.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in a site sheltered from strong wind.

directions: Unlike most Japanese maples that peak in autumn, this cultivar puts on its best show in spring, when fresh leaves open green edged in white with rose-pink mottling and a crimson leaf stalk. Plant it where morning sun and afternoon shade will protect the delicate variegation from scorching, and water regularly through its first two seasons. Every leaf comes out a little different, giving the whole canopy a shifting, multicolored look worth a prominent spot near a patio or entry.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil sheltered from drying wind; the corky bark texture develops after three to five years of growth.

directions: This Japanese maple was selected for its trunk rather than its leaves: mature bark becomes thick, corky, and deeply furrowed, giving the tree striking winter presence long after the bright green, gold-turning foliage has dropped. Grow it in light shade to protect the leaves from summer scorch, watering regularly during dry spells. Site it where the textured bark is visible in the off-season, such as along a path or near a window with a winter view.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in a spot sheltered from hot afternoon sun to keep the burgundy color from bleaching.

directions: A narrowly upright Japanese maple that stays columnar while young before filling out with age, this cultivar opens bright crimson in spring and deepens to rich burgundy through summer, finishing in scarlet come fall. Its tight habit makes it a good fit for narrow side yards or container culture where a full-size Japanese maple would not fit. Keep soil evenly moist and shelter it from strong wind, which can tatter the fine foliage.

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil; this maple tolerates more cold than most Japanese maples, making it a hardier substitute.

directions: Still uncommon in nurseries but increasingly available, this smaller maple from Korea and northern China resembles a Japanese maple in form with multi-lobed leaves that open fresh green and deepen through the season before turning red, orange, and yellow in fall. It handles more cold than most Japanese maple cultivars, making it a good choice for colder gardens that still want that refined look. Plant in light shade with protection from harsh winter wind, and water only occasionally once roots are established.

planting.note: Transplant grafted stock in spring in deep, well-drained soil; its narrow mature footprint suits street tree and tight-lot planting.

directions: Apollo is a semi-dwarf sugar maple that reaches only about half the width of a typical seedling tree while keeping a strong, straight central trunk. The dense pillar of summer foliage shifts to a spire of orange and gold in autumn, giving classic sugar maple color in a footprint that fits a city lot or narrow planting strip. Water regularly through establishment in its first few summers, and avoid compacted or salt-exposed sites that stress sugar maples generally.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in open or dappled shade; this snakebark maple needs protection from hot, dry exposure.

directions: This selection was chosen for its boldly striped chalky white and green bark, which lights up a shaded corner of the garden year-round but is especially striking against dark evergreens in winter. It grows into a broad, vase-shaped medium tree, so give it room to spread rather than crowding it against a wall. Plant in humus-rich soil with filtered or open shade and keep roots cool with a layer of mulch, since this is a true understory species that resents hot, exposed sites.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained woodland soil; more sun deepens the purple foliage color but calls for more frequent watering.

directions: A compact selection of the Pacific Northwest native vine maple, this cultivar carries smoldering reddish-purple leaves and stems through the growing season, with the color holding best when it gets a few hours of direct sun. In fall the foliage shifts to scarlet, pumpkin, and gold for a second season of interest. It stays noticeably smaller than wild vine maple, making it a good choice for understory planting beneath taller trees or as a specimen in a smaller woodland garden.

planting.note: Transplant in spring in moist to average soil; its strong central leader and narrow form suit street and narrow-lot planting.

directions: Bowhall is a narrow, upright selection of red maple prized for reliable red, orange, and burgundy fall color on a tree that fits tight spaces where a wide-spreading maple would not. Its symmetrical branching and strong central leader give it good resistance to storm damage over time. It adapts to a range of soils and tolerates urban pollution reasonably well, needing only occasional watering once established.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil; this maple is notably tough and tolerates urban conditions with non-aggressive roots safe near paving.

directions: This durable small maple earns its common name from the knobby, textured bark that becomes especially decorative on bare winter branches. Fine-textured, small leaves cast dappled shade through the season and reliably turn apricot and gold in fall, even in shadier spots, a trait that sets it apart from showier maples that need full sun for good color. It resists most pests and disease and tolerates urban soils, making it a reliable pick for a smaller garden or street-side planting.

planting.note: Plant in average, well-drained soil; established trees tolerate dry spells and urban street conditions well.

directions: A tough, handsome small tree, Lavalle hawthorn holds glossy dark green leaves well into winter and produces white flower clusters in late spring that ripen into long-lasting orange-red fruit against the lustrous foliage. It shrugs off dry soil and urban stress once established, making it a reliable street or specimen tree where many ornamentals struggle. Site it where winter fruit display can be appreciated, since the berries often persist after leaf drop.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil; this slow-growing form is ideal where space is too tight for a standard ginkgo.

directions: Gold Spire packs the classic ginkgo fan-shaped leaf and brilliant yellow fall color into an unusually tall, narrow silhouette, making it well suited to tight courtyards, narrow strips beside driveways, or formal rows where a full-width ginkgo would overwhelm the space. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, and compacted soil with ease, needing only occasional deep watering. Give it full sun for the densest form, though it tolerates some open shade.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil; this magnolia grows quickly and flowers at a young age compared to many magnolia species.

directions: A hybrid between Magnolia kobus and M. salicifolia, this selection was named for Japanese nurseryman Koichiro Wada and bears pure white flowers up to seven inches across in a profuse early spring display. Bronze-tinted new growth matures to green through summer before turning gold in fall, and the tree develops a distinctly pyramidal shape that stands apart from the typically rounded form of most magnolias. Plant in a sheltered spot with light shade from hot afternoon sun, and expect flowering at a younger age than many magnolia species.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; this crabapple is notably disease-resistant and widely used as a breeding parent for that reason.

directions: Golden Raindrops is a graceful small crabapple with finely divided, lacy foliage and a profusion of small white spring flowers, but its real signature is the fall and winter fruit display: masses of tiny golden-yellow crabapples that blush red after frost and persist for months. Its disease resistance is outstanding, and its slender, horizontally spreading limbs give the tree an elegant structure even in winter. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and expect only occasional watering once roots are established.

planting.note: Plant in moist, acidic to neutral soil; a strong central leader gives this selection a more uniform shape than typical seedling black tupelo.

directions: Afterburner lives up to its name with glossy summer foliage that ignites into scarlet, orange, and yellow in fall, arguably the best fall color of any tupelo selection. Unlike seedling-grown black tupelo, which can be gawky and irregular, this cultivar grows with a strong central leader into a uniform, pyramidal shape. It adapts to moist or acidic soils and tolerates both wet bottomland conditions and ordinary garden soil, watered regularly through its first few years.

planting.note: Transplant in spring; this selection tolerates compacted soil, pruning, and street-side planting better than most shade trees.

directions: Emerald Avenue is a refined hornbeam selection with a strong central leader and a notably uniform, upright-oval silhouette that holds its shape with little pruning. Dense, glossy dark green leaves give a tailored, formal look through the growing season and turn handsome gold tones in fall. It is exceptionally adaptable to urban soils and tolerates shearing well, making it a strong choice for formal allées, screening, or streetscape planting.

planting.note: Plant in average, well-drained soil; this narrow columnar form fits tight planting strips where a typical cornelian cherry would spread too wide.

directions: Saffron Sentinel brings the earliest flower show of any small tree in this list: clusters of bright yellow flowers open on bare branches in late winter, well before most other trees stir, followed later by edible golden-yellow fruit. Its narrow, columnar habit makes it useful for tight urban lots, foundation plantings, or anywhere a wide canopy would crowd nearby structures. It is tough and low-maintenance once established, tolerating a range of soils with only occasional supplemental water.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil; the narrow habit makes this a good vertical accent for tight spaces that still want strong fall color.

directions: This narrow, columnar form of Persian ironwood delivers the species' signature four-season interest in a fraction of the width, making it practical as a vertical accent or screen in a small garden. New leaves emerge tinged red and purple before maturing to glossy green and then flaming gold, orange, and scarlet in fall, while smooth gray bark exfoliates attractively as the tree ages. It is tough and drought-tolerant once established, with small, understated spring flowers adding an extra touch of early-season interest.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil; growth is quick for its first decade before slowing, and it often develops a handsome multi-stemmed form.

directions: This Patagonian native carries small, round, dark green leaves on a delicate, layered branching pattern that casts a light, open shade gardeners can plant right underneath. Young bark shows a distinctive cherry-like pattern that matures into an interesting scaly texture on older trunks, adding winter character. It grows quickly for its first several years before settling into a slower pace, and tolerates ordinary garden soil with only occasional watering once established.

planting.note: Plant against sturdy, permanent support such as a pergola or arbor, since mature wisteria vines become heavy and long-lived.

directions: Also sold as 'Alba', this white-flowered Japanese wisteria produces pendant racemes up to two feet long that hang beautifully from an overhead structure, releasing a sweet fragrance that draws bees and butterflies in late spring. It twines vigorously, so train it onto a pergola, arbor, or strong fence from the start and prune hard each winter to control size and encourage flowering. Pinnately compound leaves turn soft yellow in fall for a secondary season of interest.

planting.note: Plant where it can scramble through a large shrub or small tree rather than smothering a trellis, since its open habit suits that style of support.

directions: Bred at the University of British Columbia, this clematis produces nodding, bell-shaped lemon-yellow flowers on dark purple stems, each bloom marked with a small red blush at its base. It flowers sporadically on new growth through summer after an initial main flush, and the fluffy seed heads that follow add another month or two of garden interest. Its loose, open growth habit makes it well suited to climbing through a large shrub or small tree rather than a tight trellis.

planting.note: Plant on a small trellis or obelisk; this compact clematis does not need the tall support a vigorous climber would.

directions: Six-inch, bicolor flowers edged in dark pink fading to lavender toward the center make this compact clematis hard to miss, with a bright tuft of yellow stamens for contrast. It blooms over an unusually long window, flowering first in early summer and again in late summer into fall, with attractive fluffy seed heads extending interest further still. Its small stature makes it a good fit for a modest trellis, obelisk, or large container.

planting.note: Plant in a container or small bed against a modest trellis; this older cultivar stays compact enough for both.

directions: An heirloom clematis dating back well over a century, this cultivar bears large, satiny white, semi-double flowers up to seven inches wide in early summer, followed by a second flush of single blooms in late summer. Brown stamens at the center of each flower provide a soft contrast against the creamy petals. Its manageable size makes it a dependable choice for a smaller garden bed or container, where it will reliably repeat its performance year after year.

planting.note: Plant against a small trellis or obelisk in rich, well-drained soil; this vigorous Polish-bred cultivar flowers reliably in its first year.

directions: Bred in Poland, this clematis is among the most vigorous of the large-flowered reddish-purple cultivars, producing six-inch single blooms with a velvety texture and dark purple undertones. It flowers heavily in early summer and again prolifically in late summer into fall, giving two strong displays per season. Its compact size still fits a smaller garden or container despite its vigorous flowering, making it a reliable choice for gardeners who want saturated color without a sprawling vine.

planting.note: Plant at the base of a shrub, perennial, or small wire support, or let it ramble through low companions, since it does not climb on its own.

directions: Unlike typical climbing clematis, this cultivar grows more like a perennial, reaching only three to four feet tall each year and dying back to the base over winter before regrowing in spring. Royal purple flowers appear in a dense flush in early summer and continue sporadically for weeks afterward. Since it lacks true climbing tendrils, support it with a low shrub, sturdy perennial, or small wire frame, or let it spill casually along the ground among low companions.

planting.note: Plant against a strong, permanent surface such as a masonry wall, retaining wall, or mature tree trunk, since it clings by aerial roots and grows heavy with age.

directions: Native to Taiwan and the Philippines and still uncommon in gardens, this evergreen vine clings by aerial roots and offers bronze-tinted new growth against deep green older foliage year-round. It is slow to reach flowering size but rewards patience with large, lacy white blooms resembling a lacecap hydrangea in early summer, held on side branches that create a layered, three-dimensional effect against its support. It is one of the few vines that flowers well in shade, making it a good option for a north-facing wall, harsh retaining wall, or a tall tree trunk in a woodland setting.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring in moist, humus-rich soil; this clumping grass stays upright well even through heavy regional rainfall.

directions: This tidy, clump-forming moor grass is one of the earliest ornamental grasses to flower, sending up airy inflorescences above tufted foliage in a graceful, upright display. It grows well in sun or part shade and stays reliably upright through wet weather rather than flopping, making it a good fit for a mixed border or the edge of a woodland path. In fall the whole plant turns a warm gold that glows especially well when backlit by low afternoon sun.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil; established plants need only occasional watering and resent heavy, waterlogged ground.

directions: A New Zealand native grass-like evergreen perennial, red tussock grass forms soft, open mounds of thin leaves that shift from metallic golden tan to a coppery red depending on light and season, with beige tips and coppery bases emerging in winter. The fine, graceful foliage moves readily in the slightest breeze, giving it a living, textural presence in the border. Grow it in well-drained soil with only occasional watering, and use it as a textural accent among perennials or in a gravel garden.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil, including tough urban soils; it tolerates drought once established and is often grown among rocks.

directions: Sometimes still sold under its older names, this low, ground-hugging cotoneaster sculpts itself tightly around rocks, making it a natural for rockeries and the tops of retaining walls. Small, dark evergreen leaves set off the tiny white spring flowers and the bright red berries that follow in fall and often persist into winter. It tolerates a wide range of soils, including compacted urban ground, and needs only occasional watering once established.

planting.note: Plant divisions in well-drained soil; this diminutive lady's mantle spreads as a very low mat rather than clumping upward like its larger relatives.

directions: This miniature relative of common lady's mantle hugs the ground with delicate, lobed leaves that catch and hold raindrops in the same sparkling way as its larger cousins, but on a much smaller scale suited to path edges and rock garden crevices. Tiny clusters of yellow-green flowers appear in summer above the fine-textured foliage. It spreads steadily into a dense, low mat in well-drained soil, offering an unusual fine-textured alternative to the typical bigger lady's mantle groundcovers.

planting.note: Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil for edging, containers, or the front of a border; it is far more compact than standard lady's mantle.

directions: A compact, refined version of lady's mantle, this dwarf species carries scalloped, blue-green leaves that elegantly catch and hold water droplets after rain or morning dew. Delicate sprays of yellow-green flowers rise above the foliage in summer, adding a soft, airy texture without the bulk of the larger species. Its small size makes it well suited to border edging, container plantings, or tucking between stepping stones, and it tolerates a wide range of ordinary garden soils.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; mass several together for the strongest winter groundcover effect.

directions: Among the most dependable winter heaths, Springwood White smothers its bright green, needle-like foliage in small, grey-white, urn-shaped flowers from December through May, exactly when little else is blooming. Its low, trailing habit makes it a strong evergreen groundcover for a sunny bank or the edge of a retaining wall, and the flexible stems work well cascading over a wall edge or filling a winter container. Give it well-drained, slightly acidic soil and water during dry spells to keep it looking fresh.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; bronze winter foliage color pairs well with the late-winter flower show.

directions: First collected in the Swiss Alps in the early twentieth century, Vivellii winter heath covers itself in small purplish-pink flowers that deepen to magenta from January into May. Its medium green, needle-like leaves take on a bronze cast in cold weather, adding color even between bloom cycles. The slightly irregular branch spacing gives the low, spreading plant pleasant textural interest, and it works well massed as a sunny groundcover or tucked into a winter container display.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; this hybrid heath tolerates slightly more alkaline soil than Erica carnea cultivars.

directions: A cross between Erica carnea 'Myretoun Ruby' and E. erigena 'Brightness', this upright, bushy winter heath produces clear reddish-purple, bell-shaped flowers from December into April, held along stems at slightly varying angles for added texture. The compact, bushy habit makes it a strong candidate for mass planting as a winter groundcover, where the evergreen foliage disappears beneath the flush of bloom. Bees visit readily on mild winter days, making it a useful early-season nectar source as well as a garden display.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; this vigorous, mounding heath has been a reliable Pacific Northwest performer for decades.

directions: Found in Germany in the early twentieth century, Silberschmelze translates roughly as 'molten silver,' a fitting name for the sea of small, bell-shaped, silvery-white flowers that cover this heath from December into May. Mid-green, needle-like foliage disappears beneath the bloom at peak flowering, and the compact, mounding habit makes it well suited to mass planting as a sunny winter groundcover. Established plants are reliably long-lived and require little more than an occasional trim after flowering to keep a neat shape.

planting.note: Plant in sandy or rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; bell heather tolerates leaner, grittier conditions than winter heath.

directions: Found near Broadstone in Dorset, England, this bell heather selection blooms from June through September, offering a summer counterpart to the winter-blooming Erica carnea cultivars. Urn-shaped, bright magenta flowers cover the dark green foliage, which is arranged in distinctive rolled whorls of three along each stem. It is notably more tolerant of sandy or rocky soil than winter heath, making it a neat, drought-tolerant groundcover choice for lean, exposed sites.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil; this shrub tolerates shearing well and is often used as a sun-loving substitute for golden boxwood.

directions: This small-leaved honeysuckle shrub forms a mound of arching branches covered in tiny golden leaves that take on a bright, almost platinum cast in full sun and deepen to chartreuse with more shade. It tolerates shearing readily, making it a popular golden substitute for boxwood in low hedges and simple topiary shapes, or it can be left loose as a tall, mounding groundcover beneath larger trees. Water occasionally during dry spells once the shrub is established.

planting.note: Plant divisions in lean, well-drained soil; this stonecrop thrives in hot, dry sites with poor soil that discourage most other groundcovers.

directions: This selection of Kamchatka stonecrop forms a dense, flat carpet of glossy green leaves that is virtually maintenance-free once established, thriving in exactly the hot, dry, poor-soil conditions that frustrate many other groundcovers. Clusters of golden yellow flowers open in late summer and age to orange through fall, extending seasonal color well past most other succulent groundcovers. It works equally well edging a dry border, filling gaps in a rock garden, or spilling from a container.

planting.note: Plant divisions in lean, well-drained soil; it performs best in hot, dry sites with poor soil rather than rich garden beds.

directions: A flat, dense-mounding stonecrop with mid-green leaves softly covered in tiny hairs, this species produces cheerful clusters of yellow flowers in late summer above the tidy foliage mat. It thrives in hot, dry sites with lean soil where richer plantings would struggle, making it a dependable choice for a rock garden or the edge of a dry border. It also performs well in containers, needing little more than good drainage and occasional water during extended dry spells.

planting.note: Plant divisions in lean, well-drained soil; pink flowers appear unusually late in the season, extending fall color in a rock garden.

directions: Known commonly as October daphne for its late pink flowers, this stonecrop forms a flat, dense mound of rounded blue-green leaves arranged in whorls along trailing stems. It thrives in hot, dry sites with lean soil, where it needs little care beyond good drainage, and its rosy-pink fall flower clusters arrive later than most other sedums, extending seasonal color into autumn. It suits a rock garden, dry border edge, or trailing container planting equally well.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in lean, well-drained soil; this groundcover roots readily where stems touch soil.

directions: This two-row stonecrop selection carries small, scalloped leaves flushed red over green, forming a durable, weed-smothering evergreen mat only a few inches tall. Small red flowers rise just above the foliage in fall, adding a bright finishing layer of color to the carpet below. It is well suited to tucking into rock wall crevices, filling spare geometric containers alongside other succulents, or planting in troughs and alpine garden beds.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil; left unstaked it spreads flat over the ground or down a slope, or it can be staked upright and trained.

directions: This unusual selection of native western hemlock has entirely lost its upright habit, instead flowing in long, trailing branches that can be left to hug the ground, cascade over rocks, or spill down a retaining wall. With staking and patient training, it can also be grown as a small weeping standard with branches streaming down from a chosen height. Either way, it brings a soft, textured, evergreen presence that few other conifers can match in a shaded groundcover role.

planting.note: Plant in cracks and crevices of a rock wall or along a gravel path, where its vigorous trailing habit can soften hard edges.

directions: A vigorous selection of Serbian bellflower, Blue Waterfall was chosen for larger leaves and a heavier, longer-lasting show of blue star-shaped flowers than the standard species. It flowers from late spring well into summer, forming a tough flowering groundcover that tolerates being walked near and squeezed into tight spots. Use it to fill cracks and crevices in a rock wall, soften the edges of a gravel path, or cascade over the top of a retaining wall.

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade; it spreads slowly, so give it time to establish before expecting full coverage.

directions: Unusual among hardy maidenhair ferns for staying evergreen through winter, this delicate-looking but tough little fern unfurls new fronds in late winter with a warm bronze blush before settling into fresh spring green. It spreads slowly into a gentle groundcover, making it well suited to lining a shaded path or filling the gaps between larger woodland perennials without becoming invasive. Plant in humus-rich soil with filtered light, and keep it consistently but not excessively moist.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes or divisions in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in shade; foliage goes dormant in midsummer, so mark the spot.

directions: This whimsical woodland perennial earns its common name from small maroon-and-white flowers with tail-like tips that peek out from beneath the leaves in April, looking uncannily like the back ends of tiny mice scurrying into the undergrowth. Its glossy, spade-shaped leaves form a low groundcover through spring before going dormant in midsummer, so it pairs well with spring-flowering woodland bulbs that can fill the gap later in the season. Plant it in deep shade under trees or shrubs where children and adults alike can be surprised by its curious blooms.
